title: What We Want to Achieve
body:
This dataset represents one of the largest and fastest-growing bodies of evidence on how public servants think about, learn, use, and adapt to emerging AI technologies. Despite the growing importance of AI in public service, most government employees receive little or no training in these skills. We also lack a structured understanding of their attitudes toward AI tools. Our research helps fill this long-standing gap by providing one of the first large-scale datasets on how public servants perceive, learn, and adapt to new technologies.

This scale gives us an unusually detailed picture of how training, especially in AI, shapes public sector work.

Analyses of this rich data allow us to observe how workers acquire foundational AI literacy, which skills are most readily adopted, how attitudes shift over time, and which organizational constraints enable or impede effective use. Because we track behavior and attitudes before training, immediately after instruction, and again several months later, we endeavor to distinguish short-term learning gains from durable changes in capability and confidence.

Situated within the broader field of AI and work, our research program serves as a real-time observatory for understanding:

  • The tasks public servants perform with AI and barriers to effective use
  • How structured learning reshapes those behaviors
  • How workers believe these changes will influence organizational performance, service delivery, and public value creation more generally

Our core hypothesis is that targeted investments in public sector human capital—training government employees to use AI tools responsibly and effectively—lead to measurable improvements in government operations and, ultimately, better outcomes for residents. Skill training is not peripheral to government performance. Rather, it is central to creating institutions that are more effective, responsive, and deserving of public trust.

Our broader aim is to understand the full pathway from learning to impact: whether investments in upskilling lead to changes in day-to-day behavior, whether those behaviors strengthen organizational capacity, and whether that increased capacity results in better outcomes for residents.

title: What We Cannot Answer Yet
body:
While our survey data are extensive, important constraints limit the analyses we can currently perform. Measures of key constructs and competencies are generally consistent across our large respondent base, but demographic and job role data vary across programs, and most data lack individual-level identifiers. This means we cannot systematically examine how outcomes differ by participant characteristics, nor can we link respondents across survey waves to track change over time. Instead, we must rely on aggregate comparisons.
 


Additionally, our performance measures are entirely self-reported, meaning that we do not currently have access to objective performance metrics or administrative data that would allow us to validate self-assessments against actual work outcomes. These gaps inform our plans to acquire external data and refine our survey instruments in future iterations.

title: What We Aim to Study in 2026
body:
To fully understand the conditions for successful AI adoption in government, some critical questions require outside datasets, including:

Policy Environment

Do states or cities with pro-AI policies have higher adoption or stronger outcomes?

We aim to link external data on statewide AI strategies, union representation and other policy differences and assess how these policies correlate with usage, confidence, and skill adoption.

Access

Do workers have AI tools available at the desktop or through enterprise systems?

Skill alone is not enough; access determines actual adoption. We have access to information on desktop availability of AI, permitted and banned tools.

Usage Patterns

How often do workers use AI tools?

In some states, we have access to anonymized usage logs of statewide AI platforms (e.g. cloud-based enterprise-wide AI) that tell us how much people are using AI.

External Attitudes and Trust

How do our findings compare to other national surveys?

We intend to connect our results with other surveys states and cities are administering to their workers.

Organizational Outcomes

How do changes in worker behavior correlate with operational metrics?

This requires administrative or performance data such as processing times, error rates, resident satisfaction, cost or time savings, productivity indicators that will require careful experiment design.

Ultimately, the goal of this research is to understand whether investments in workforce upskilling translate into meaningful changes in how public servants work—and whether those changes strengthen the capacity of government institutions.

By connecting individual learning gains to shifts in behavior, workflow, and organizational performance, we aim to evaluate how training can contribute to more effective public services and better outcomes for residents.
